faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Mays Landing chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. The village chimneys are mostly older brick, and several have lost their caps to storms over the years. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Mays Landing garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. River-bottom gardens here sit on soft, diggable soil, and a resident groundhog usually dens under the nearest shed or porch rather than out in the open. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

Mays Landing.wildlife_intro:
Mays Landing still reads as a river village: the Great Egg Harbor River curls past the old courthouse blocks, Lake Lenape sits at the west end, and streets of 1800s and early-1900s houses give way to postwar subdivisions along Routes 40 and 50. That older housing is where the work concentrates. Raccoons den in uncapped chimneys on the village streets, big brown bats summer in the tall attics of the riverfront-era homes, and groundhogs work the garden lots that back onto open ground toward Weymouth and the river bottom.

Masonry chimneys deserve a slow look. Mortar joints crumble at the crown, flashing lifts where the stack meets the roof, and an uncapped flue reads to a raccoon like a hollow tree. Sealing here is masonry work as much as animal work: a correctly sized cap, repointed joints where they have failed, and flashing reset so water stays out along with the wildlife. Brick and stone stacks on older houses often hide a second, unused flue that nobody remembers — exactly the sort of quiet, warm shaft a denning animal chooses in March. In Mays Landing the inspection always includes the flue and the river-side foundation wall, because those are the two routes village animals have used for a century.

faqs.q: What snakes turn up around Hammonton, and which are dangerous?
faqs.a: This is Pine Barrens snake country. The northern pine snake — state-Threatened, a burrower in sandy soil — is the species people meet most dramatically, and it is protected: identification and referral, never handling. A separate southern population of timber rattlesnakes also persists in the Barrens. Sandy Hammonton soil is exactly what a pine snake wants for burrowing, so a big pale snake near a woodpile here deserves a photograph and a wide berth, not a shovel. Common harmless residents include black racers, garter snakes, and eastern hognose, which plays dead theatrically. Non-listed snakes found inside a home can be caught and released outdoors within 200 meters.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Hammonton foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. In Hammonton the burrow undermining a barn slab or a farmhouse addition is the common version of this call, and the field edge behind the building is usually where the second entrance sits. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

Hammonton.wildlife_intro:
Hammonton calls itself the Blueberry Capital of the World, and the working farms that ring the town shape its wildlife calls as much as the houses do. Along the White Horse Pike and the downtown blocks the housing is older frame and brick; out past the town line, farmhouses and ranch homes sit between blueberry fields and the pitch-pine edge of the Barrens. Groundhogs commute between field edges and foundation burrows, raccoons work barn lofts and chimneys, and at the sandy Barrens fringe the occasional pine snake sighting sends a homeowner indoors to make a phone call.

On farm and acreage properties the house is only part of the job. Barns shelter raccoon families in haylofts, groundhogs undermine run-in sheds and fence lines, and skunks take up residence under equipment sheds where they are discovered by smell. We plan the property as a whole — which structures to proof, which burrows to treat, where trapping effort actually pays — instead of chasing one animal at a time. Grain and feed storage gets the same attention as the house foundation, because spilled feed is usually what drew the animals to the buildings in the first place. Hammonton jobs are quoted as a property, not a single structure, because the barn, the shed, and the house usually share the same animals.
